title: Maximal Number of Repetitions at Percentages of the One Repetition Maximum: A Meta-Regression and Moderator Analysis of Sex, Age, Training Status, and Exercise
authors: Nuzzo JL, Pinto MD, Nosaka K, Steele J
population: 952 repetitions-to-failure tests in 7289 individuals in 452 groups from 269 studies; 66% male, 97% healthy, 92% under 59 years, 60% resistance trained; the bench press (42%) and the leg press (14%) were the most studied exercises
findings: A meta-regression estimated the mean and the between-individuals standard deviation of the number of repetitions completed to failure at each percentage of the one repetition maximum (1RM).
The mean repetitions were best described by natural cubic splines and the standard deviation by a linear model, and both fell as the percentage of 1RM rose.

More repetitions were completed in the leg press than the bench press across the loading range, so separate tables were built for these two exercises; the authors found little influence of sex, age or training status and so give one general table for all other exercises.
The authors note that more data are needed for tables of other exercises.
limitations: Few studies cover lower-body free-weight lifts such as the squat or the Romanian deadlift; the abstract gives no table values; the tests were to failure in healthy, mostly young adults. Abstract read on Europe PMC (open access); the tables were not read.
implications: The number of repetitions possible at a given percentage of the maximum is not linear and varies between people and exercises, so an equation that converts repetitions to a maximum is an approximation. The engine uses the linear form only for a starting load, a ceiling and a labelled estimate (f8.e1rmDivisor), never for a test.
No sex, age or training-status adjustment is supported by this analysis, consistent with the rule that sex never changes the dose.
